teaser: A half-open eye, a boat with no rower, and a Salon that blushed.
review_notes:
IMAGE MISMATCH: the image appears to be the smaller, sketchier version of the composition in the National Gallery, London (about 96 x 130 cm, proportions 4:3), not the large Salon painting in the Petit Palais (174 x 206 cm, more nearly square, more finished, with a man's hat in the boat). Coordinates are placed on the supplied image; the lesson only points at features both versions share and gives the Petit Palais dimensions. If the image is replaced, all coordinates must be redone.
The brunette as being in her underclothes (chemise and petticoats, lying on her dress): standard reading of the Salon picture.
Proudhon's moralising commentary on the picture (in his posthumous book on art, 1865): paraphrased.
Manet's Luncheon on the Grass dated 1863.
Courbet's months of flower painting at Etienne Baudry's in Saintonge, 1862.

lesson.text: The moment is this: a woman lying in the grass has heard something. Her eyelids lift, not all the way, just enough to see who is there. Her friend has not moved yet. In a second one of them will speak, or sit up, or pull a shawl over herself. Courbet stops the clock right before.

It is a hot summer afternoon on the Seine, somewhere outside Paris. By the 1850s new railway lines let city people reach the river in under an hour, and Sunday on the water was becoming a habit: rowing, eating, napping under the trees. Nobody had yet thought it worth a large painting.

Courbet did. He showed the picture at the Salon of 1857, the big official exhibition in Paris, on a canvas about 1.74 by 2.06 meters (roughly 5 feet 8 by 6 feet 9). The women were close to life-size, sprawled at the visitors' feet. The crowd pressed in, and many did not like what they understood.

The title was a provocation. A “demoiselle” was a well-bred unmarried young lady. Applied to two women lying half undressed on a public riverbank, the word sounded sarcastic, and everyone in 1857 heard the joke.

Why half undressed? The dark-haired woman in front has taken off her dress in the heat. What she wears, the gauzy sleeves and the white skirts spilling toward you, is what went underneath. To a public used to nudes disguised as goddesses, a real Parisian in her underclothes was far more indecent.

And they did not walk here. Somewhere behind them, Courbet painted how they arrived. It is easy to miss, because it has almost the same brown as the tree trunks and sits low against the blue of the water.
How did the two women get to this spot? The answer is in the background.

spots.title: The boat
spots.text: A rowboat is tied up at the bank, empty. Two women in heavy skirts did not row it alone, viewers reasoned. So where is the third person?

lesson.text: That absent rower is the engine of the scandal. If someone brought them, then someone is nearby. Go back to the first second of this lesson, the eyes that open because a person is approaching. The simplest answer to “where is he?” is: standing exactly where you are.

lesson.title: What she sees, what you see
lesson.text: Three details change meaning once you take the visitor's place.

spots.title: The half-open eyes
spots.text: Her head rests on her arm, cheeks flushed with heat. The eyes are slits, heavy but not asleep, and they are turned toward the viewer. Critics called the look shameless.

spots.title: The yellow glove
spots.text: Her dress is off, but she has kept her gloves on. That mix of fashion and undress is what made her look, to 1857 eyes, like a woman of doubtful morals instead of a tired picnicker.

spots.title: The friend
spots.text: The blonde sits up fully dressed, in a wide pale hat and a coral bracelet, chin on her hand. She stares off to the left, bored or dreaming. She has not noticed anyone.

lesson.text: So the picture holds two different times at once. For the blonde, nothing is happening. For the brunette, something has just begun. You, the viewer, are the event. Few paintings before this one had given the person looking such an awkward part to play.
Courbet painted modern leisure with no myth to excuse it and no story to explain it. He leaves a gap, the missing companion, and lets the viewer fall into it.

The heap of flowers in the blonde's lap was picked on the spot, and nobody is looking at it. Courbet enjoyed such passages for their own sake: a few years later, staying with a friend who loved gardening, he spent whole months painting almost nothing but flowers.

The philosopher Pierre-Joseph Proudhon, a friend of the painter, tried to rescue the picture by turning it into a sermon. For him these were two idle, kept women, proof of how money was rotting French society under the Emperor. Courbet let him talk. His paint says something less tidy: it lingers on the lace and the warm skin with obvious pleasure.
Courbet worked the idea out more than once. Besides the big Salon canvas kept in Paris, a smaller, looser version of the same two women belongs to the National Gallery in London.

Six years later, Édouard Manet sat two clothed men and a naked woman on a riverbank and caused the biggest art scandal of the century. A decade after that, Monet and Renoir were setting up their easels by the same river to paint boaters and bathers. The Sunday afternoon that shocked the Salon of 1857 had become the favorite subject of a new generation.

quiz.question: Why did the title sound ironic in 1857?
options: “Demoiselles” suggested respectable young ladies, which these women did not seem to be
The scene is not really on the Seine
The women were in fact married
quiz.explanation: A polite word was applied to women lying half undressed in public.

quiz.question: What is the dark-haired woman wearing?
options: Her underclothes, with gloves still on
quiz.explanation: She has taken off her dress in the heat but kept her yellow gloves.

quiz.question: What detail suggests that someone else is nearby?
options: A man's shadow on the grass
An empty rowboat tied to the bank
quiz.explanation: The boat implies a rower who is not shown.

quiz.question: What is the blonde woman doing?
options: Looking away to the left, chin on her hand
quiz.explanation: She sits up, dressed, and has not noticed anyone approaching.

quiz.question: Which later painter set a scandalous picnic on a riverbank six years afterward?
quiz.explanation: Manet's Luncheon on the Grass followed in 1863.

facts.text: The painting was shown at the Paris Salon of 1857.
facts.explanation: It was exhibited there and drew crowds and criticism.

facts.text: The two women are shown as goddesses from Greek myth.
facts.explanation: They are contemporary Parisians, with no myth to excuse the scene.

facts.text: Both women are looking straight at the viewer.
facts.explanation: Only the brunette's half-open eyes turn our way; the blonde looks off to the side.
